title: Find the Prefix Common Array of Two Arrays
spaceBreakdown:
- maskA (unsigned long long): one 64-bit integer → O(1)
- maskB (unsigned long long): one 64-bit integer → O(1)
- C (returned vector): not counted
- No recursion, no other containers
approach: Since A and B are permutations of 1..n with n ≤ 50, we track which values have appeared in each array using a 64-bit bitmask. At each index i, set bit A[i] in maskA and bit B[i] in maskB, then C[i] = popcount(maskA & maskB). This is correct because a value is "common at or before i" exactly when it has appeared in both prefixes, and the AND of the two masks captures precisely those values.
hints: With only n ≤ 50 distinct values ever appearing, how compactly can you represent the entire set of values seen so far in one array?

Use a 64-bit integer as a bitmask for each array. At index i, set bit A[i] in maskA and bit B[i] in maskB; C[i] = popcount(maskA & maskB). In Example 1 at i=1, maskA has bits {1,3}, maskB has bits {3,1}, AND has 2 bits set, so C[1]=2.

```
maskA = 0, maskB = 0
for i from 0 to n-1:
    maskA |= 1 << A[i]
    maskB |= 1 << B[i]
    C[i] = popcount(maskA & maskB)
return C
```

**Smallest input** - n=1, both arrays contain the single value 1.
`A = [1], B = [1]` → `Expected: [1]`
⚠️ Bug: initializing C[0] to 0 and skipping the loop body → returns [0]

**Largest bit position** - n=50, value 50 requires bit 50 in the mask.
`A = [50,1,2,...,49], B = [50,1,2,...,49]` → `Expected: [1,2,3,...,50]`
⚠️ Bug: using a 32-bit int for the mask (1 << 50 overflows int) → undefined behavior, wrong counts

**First elements differ** - no value is common at index 0.
`A = [1,3,2,4], B = [3,1,2,4]` → `Expected: [0,2,3,4]`
⚠️ Bug: using popcount(maskA | maskB) instead of popcount(maskA & maskB) → at i=0 returns 2 instead of 0

**Last index always full** - for any two permutations, C[n-1] = n.
`A = [2,3,1], B = [3,1,2]` → `Expected: [0,1,3]`
⚠️ Bug: looping to n-2 instead of n-1 → C[n-1] left uninitialized, returns garbage

followUps.q: What if n can be up to 10^5?
followUps.a: A 64-bit bitmask can no longer hold all values. Switch to a frequency array of size n+1 and a running counter: increment freq[A[i]] and freq[B[i]]; whenever a frequency reaches exactly 2, increment the counter and set C[i] to it. O(n) time, O(n) space.

followUps.q: What if the arrays arrive as a stream and you cannot store them?
followUps.a: The bitmask approach still works online - process each (A[i], B[i]) pair as it arrives, update the two masks, and emit C[i] immediately. Beyond the output buffer, auxiliary space stays O(1).

followUps.q: What if A and B are not guaranteed to be permutations (duplicates or missing values allowed)?
followUps.a: The bitmask breaks because a duplicate in one array sets the same bit twice with no effect. Use a frequency array and count a value as common only when it has appeared at least once in both arrays' prefixes, tracked by two separate boolean arrays or a single freq array with threshold 2. O(n) time, O(n) space.
